doc.title: Bill Allred interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 24, 2017

title: Adapting his playing and Turk Murphy's comment
summary: He says players tailor their style to the band and audience, recalling Turk Murphy telling him he played too many notes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I think you do. I really think you do. And thank God I had enough technical ability to be able to do that. And I guess that’s not really bragging I mean it’s just — you know I remember Turk Murphy, I sat in with Turk’s band out in San Francisco. I loved that band. I just — there was a romance about that whole San Francisco thing that I really liked it. And I was playing and got done, and we’re down in Turk’s break room where everybody’s filling up their pipes with all this magic stuff. And I never really got into that much. But Turk said, “Hey, I like the way you play, kid” he said, “you play too damn many notes though.” I said, I got a quote out of Turk. And it was a fault of mine. I wanted to play a good chorus and so maybe I was doing a little too much. Wild Bill loved it.

Our benefactor, who started this project, was a frequent attender at these jazz parties. And I recall he would say something like, he’s look at the list of musicians and go, “Oh yeah I like him, oh Watrous well too many notes.” He would say that kind of thing. And I know that certain players would sort of temper their approach when they looked out at the audience and assess what they see.

You know, and I think the ability of a player to stylize like that, I think is important. I mean I do jazz parties now, a variety of them. There’s one thing I do, the party that’s like a cruise off of Lauderdale. And the people that go on that thing, they want to hear the Dixieland stuff. They don’t care if you get a little erratic in your choruses but you do, by virtue of that, you kind of control your torrents of notes. But still then you’re going — it’s not only the complexity of what you play, it is the, it’s the tunes and the way you — you know like I’m getting ready to go to a party out in Colorado Springs that I’ve done quite a few times. And you know you’ve got to bone up, you’ve got to do some Latin tunes, you’ve got to sound like you know what you’re doing. And my son had the same problem you know. You have to stylize. But you don’t want to overdo it because they it sounds foreign, then it sounds like what the hell’s he doing.
Yeah. You’re playing down to people.
